For the square-uniform integer initialization explicitly specified in the source, the limiting probability at position zero is \(5/24\), not \(1/4\).

Choose
\[
(a_0,a_1)=(x,y)
\]
uniformly from
\[
[-N,N]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2,
\]
and extend the Fibonacci recurrence in both directions. Its neighboring terms are
\[
a_{-2}=2x-y,\qquad
a_{-1}=y-x,\qquad
a_0=x,\qquad
a_1=y,\qquad
a_2=x+y.
\]

If \(x\ne0\), put \(r=y/x\). A unique global absolute minimum at index zero requires
\[
|r|>1,
\qquad
|r-1|>1,
\qquad
|r+1|>1,
\qquad
|2-r|>1.
\]
Their intersection is exactly
\[
r<-2\quad\text{or}\quad r>3.
\]
These conditions are also sufficient. After simultaneously negating \(x,y\) if necessary, assume \(x>0\). For \(r<-2\), the forward terms have a common negative sign and strictly increasing absolute value, while the backward terms alternate signs with strictly increasing absolute value. For \(r>3\), the forward terms are positive and increasing, and the backward terms again alternate with increasing absolute value. Therefore no later index attains a smaller absolute value. The cases \(x=0\), \(y\ne0\) also have their unique minimum at index zero.

Hence the exact number of square-lattice initializations having unique minimum at zero is
\[
C_N=
2N
+
2\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor(N-1)/2\rfloor}(N-2j)
+
2\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor(N-1)/3\rfloor}(N-3j).
\]
Consequently
\[
\lim_{N\to\infty}P_N(0)
=
\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{C_N}{(2N+1)^2}
=
\frac5{24}.
\]
Since
\[
\frac5{24}\ne\frac14,
\]
the conjectured distribution contradicts its own stated square-uniform sampling rule.

The discrepancy comes from treating a uniform distribution on an expanding square as though it induced a uniform polar angle. It does not; the arctangent expression corresponds to a different rotationally invariant sampling scheme.
